items.stem: Which of the following best describes "incongruity"?
options: A mismatch between elements (e.g. serious form and trivial content) that produces humour
Exaggeration of a person's features for comic or critical effect
A gap between what is said and what is meant, or between expectation and reality
Journalism or parody news that uses humour to criticise public life
items.answer: A mismatch between elements (e.g. serious form and trivial content) that produces humour
items.markingKey: A. "incongruity" is a mismatch between elements (e.g. serious form and trivial content) that produces humour.

items.stem: Explain why satire often imitates serious genres such as news reports.
items.answer: The serious form creates incongruity with absurd content and lets the target condemn itself in its own style.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The serious form creates incongruity with absurd content and lets the target condemn itself in its own style. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between satire and parody.
items.answer: Satire criticises a target (often social or political) through humour; parody imitates a specific text or genre. Parody is often a tool of satire.
items.markingKey: Satire criticises a target (often social or political) through humour; parody imitates a specific text or genre. Parody is often a tool of satire. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following satirical column from a news-parody website.

In a bold move hailed by absolutely everyone in the Cabinet, the government announced today that the housing crisis will henceforth be known as the 'housing opportunity'. 'Language matters,' said the Minister, speaking from the second of his four homes. 'Young people aren't priced out – they're simply enjoying an extended stay with their parents, which is wonderful for family values.' A spokesperson confirmed that rents would remain the same, but would now feel more optimistic.

Identify the target of the satire and explain the methods used.
items.answer: Target: governments that replace policy with spin. Methods: a deadpan news register, mock euphemism ("housing opportunity"), ironic detail (four homes), and bathos ("feel more optimistic"); incongruity between serious form and absurd content creates the humour.
items.markingKey: Target: governments that replace policy with spin. Methods: a deadpan news register, mock euphemism ("housing opportunity"), ironic detail (four homes), and bathos ("feel more optimistic"); incongruity between serious form and absurd content creates the humour. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: "Satire is just comedy and has no serious purpose." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Satire uses comedy to criticise and provoke change; its purpose is moral or political.
items.markingKey: Satire uses comedy to criticise and provoke change; its purpose is moral or political. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Read the following parody advertisement created by a student activist group (culture jamming).

Read the following three-panel comic strip, described in words.

[Panel 1: a world leader at a podium declares, 'We pledge to reach net zero by 2050!' Applause lines fill the background.]
[Panel 2: a polar bear on a shrinking ice floe raises a paw: 'Question – what's the plan for this summer?']
[Panel 3: the leader, sweating, looks away: 'Next question.']

Discuss the relationship between image and words in this text.
items.answer: The shrinking floe beside the podium visualises urgency against political theatre; the sweating leader signals discomfort.
items.markingKey: The shrinking floe beside the podium visualises urgency against political theatre; the sweating leader signals discomfort. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following editorial cartoon, described in words.

[A pair of scales of justice. On one pan sits a tiny pile of coins labelled 'Fine for polluting the river'. On the other, a mountain of banknotes labelled 'Annual profit'. The scales tip violently towards the profit. A very small judge peers up at it and says: 'Well, that'll teach them.']

How does the text use irony and exaggeration to criticise its target?
items.answer: Target: weak corporate penalties and the legal system. Methods: visual metaphor (scales), exaggeration of scale and verbal irony.
items.markingKey: Target: weak corporate penalties and the legal system. Methods: visual metaphor (scales), exaggeration of scale and verbal irony. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: A student claims: "Parody adverts are just vandalism with no meaning." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They are deliberate texts that use intertextual techniques to critique advertising; legality aside, they communicate arguments.
items.markingKey: They are deliberate texts that use intertextual techniques to critique advertising; legality aside, they communicate arguments. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following satirical news story from a parody website.

Local man Darren Cole, 41, has once again shown extraordinary courage by sharing a news article on social media without reading beyond the headline. 'I didn't need to,' Cole explained. 'The headline already agreed with me.' Friends describe the gesture as 'very on brand'. At press time, Cole was furiously defending the article's second paragraph, which he believes says something it does not.

How does the text use humour to make a serious point?
items.answer: Target: confirmation bias and careless sharing. Methods: mock-heroic diction, an "everyman" figure, ironic self-incrimination in quotation, parody of news clichés; the reader is invited to recognise themselves.
items.markingKey: Target: confirmation bias and careless sharing. Methods: mock-heroic diction, an "everyman" figure, ironic self-incrimination in quotation, parody of news clichés; the reader is invited to recognise themselves. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following altered ("subvertised") billboard for a fictional soft drink, described in words.

[Original billboard: a smiling teenager drinks from a red can of FIZZ. Slogan: 'OPEN JOY.']
[Altered version: the word 'JOY' has been pasted over with 'DECAY' in matching lettering. A sticker beside the can reads: '35 g of sugar – that's about 9 teaspoons.' The teenager's smile has been left untouched.]

How does the text use irony and exaggeration to criticise its target?
items.answer: Culture jamming: the alteration hijacks the brand's slogan and image to expose what the advert conceals (sugar and health).
items.markingKey: Culture jamming: the alteration hijacks the brand's slogan and image to expose what the advert conceals (sugar and health). Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following parody advertisement created by a student activist group (culture jamming).

[Image: a glossy fashion-advert layout. A model in a neon crop top poses, smiling, in front of a landfill heaped with clothes.]
WEAR IT ONCE. POST IT. BIN IT.
New season, new you – every week.
*Made by someone paid less in a month than this top costs in a day.
#OutfitOfTheMinute

Analyse how the text imitates and subverts the conventions of advertising.
items.answer: Parody imitates fast-fashion advertising (layout, slogan, hashtag, small print) and exaggerates it, so the genre condemns itself; culture jamming turns the brand's language against consumption.
items.markingKey: Parody imitates fast-fashion advertising (layout, slogan, hashtag, small print) and exaggerates it, so the genre condemns itself; culture jamming turns the brand's language against consumption. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following satirical column from a news-parody website.

In a bold move hailed by absolutely everyone in the Cabinet, the government announced today that the housing crisis will henceforth be known as the 'housing opportunity'. 'Language matters,' said the Minister, speaking from the second of his four homes. 'Young people aren't priced out – they're simply enjoying an extended stay with their parents, which is wonderful for family values.' A spokesperson confirmed that rents would remain the same, but would now feel more optimistic.

Guiding question: How does the writer use the conventions of news reporting to satirise politicians?
Write one analytical paragraph that answers the guiding question, using at least two references to the text.
items.answer: Thesis: by imitating a neutral news report, the satire lets politicians condemn themselves. (1) Deadpan news structure. (2) Ironic details and quotations exposing hypocrisy. (3) Bathos in the closing line. Evaluation: humour invites agreement but may encourage cynicism rather than action.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: by imitating a neutral news report, the satire lets politicians condemn themselves. (1) Deadpan news structure. (2) Ironic details and quotations exposing hypocrisy. (3) Bathos in the closing line. Evaluation: humour invites agreement but may encourage cynicism rather than action. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: "Satire changes nothing; it only makes people laugh." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Satire rarely causes change directly, but it shapes public attitudes and holds power to account.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: audiences may enjoy satire without acting; it can breed cynicism. Arguments against: satire has exposed hypocrisy and shifted opinion; it gives voice to dissent under repression. items.stem: "Culture jamming is an effective way to challenge consumer culture." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It is effective at provoking reflection but limited in changing consumption.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it uses the brand's visibility; it provokes thought in public spaces. Arguments against: it is easily co-opted by brands; audiences may enjoy it without changing behaviour.
